---
title: "Strings & Regex"
subtitle: "≈ stringr · R4DS strings & regular expressions"
jupyter: python3
---

Every Polars string function lives in one namespace, `.str`, on an
expression. The [cheatsheet](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-strings)
maps stringr to it function by function; this chapter covers what a
one-to-one table hides. The regex engine is a different one (Rust `regex`, not
ICU), a pattern can differ per row, offsets come in two units, and Thai text
shows that a "character" is not what you see. Splitting a string into columns
is in [Reshaping](../transform/reshape.qmd#sec-rs-strings).

## In tidyverse {#sec-str-tidyverse}

```r
library(tidyverse)

x <- c("CT chest: 5 mm nodule", "MRI brain 3 T", "CT ช่องท้อง 2.5 ซม.")

str_detect(x, "CT")                          # pattern = ICU regex by default
str_detect(x, fixed("."))                    # fixed() / coll() / regex() modify it
str_extract(x, "\\d+(?= mm)")                # look-ahead: ICU supports it
str_extract(x, "(\\d+) mm", group = 1)       # or capture a group (stringr ≥ 1.5)
str_replace(x, "(\\w+) (\\w+)", "\\2 \\1")   # back-references as \\1
str_replace_all(x, c("CT" = "computed tomography", "MRI" = "magnetic resonance"))
str_length("ท้อง")                           # 4: code points, not what you see
str_sub(x, 1, 2)                             # 1-based, end inclusive
```

stringr vectorises over string *and* pattern, and the pattern is ICU regex
unless wrapped. Polars keeps the vectorisation and swaps the engine: two ICU
features are gone, `\\1` becomes `$1`, and lengths and offsets need a unit.

## Mental model {#sec-str-model}

```text
 pl.col("report").str.contains( pattern , literal=False )
 └──── Expr ────┘ └ns┘└ method ┘ └──┬──┘
                                    ├── "CT|MRI"        one pattern, compiled once, used on every row
                                    └── pl.col("pat")   one pattern per row (stringr's vectorised pattern)

 a regex pattern ──► Rust `regex` crate: linear time, Unicode-aware by default,
                                         no look-around, no back-references
```

The same `pattern` argument means different things to different methods:

| The pattern is… | Methods | stringr analogue |
|---|---|---|
| a regex; `literal=True` opts out | `contains`, `find`, `count_matches`, `replace`, `replace_all` | default; `fixed()` |
| always a regex | `extract`, `extract_all`, `extract_groups` | default |
| literal; `literal=False` opts in | `split` | — |
| always literal | `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `strip_prefix`, `strip_suffix` | `fixed()` |
| a set of characters | `strip_chars`, `strip_chars_start`, `strip_chars_end` | — |
| many literals at once (Aho-Corasick) | `contains_any`, `extract_many`, `find_many`, `replace_many` | `fixed()` + `|` |

: How `.str` methods read their pattern {.striped}

| | stringr (ICU) | Polars (Rust `regex`) |
|---|---|---|
| Look-ahead/behind `(?=…)`, `(?<=…)` | yes | parse error (@sec-str-engine) |
| Back-reference `\1` inside a pattern | yes | parse error |
| Group reference in a replacement | `\\1` | `$1`, `${name}`, `$0` (@sec-str-replace) |
| Options | `regex(ignore_case =, multiline =, dotall =, comments =)` | inline flags `(?i)`, `(?m)`, `(?s)`, `(?x)` |
| `\d`, `\w`, `\b` | Unicode | Unicode: `๑๒` is `\d` |
| `[[:alpha:]]` | Unicode | **ASCII only** |
| Positions | 1-based, end inclusive | 0-based `(offset, length)` |
| Length unit | code points | code points (`len_chars`); `find` returns **bytes** |
| Matching | backtracking | linear time in the input, no catastrophic patterns |

: The engines side by side {.striped}

## Mechanics {#sec-str-mechanics}

```{python}
#| include: false
%xmode Minimal
```

```{python}
import re

import polars as pl
from pl_notes import datasets

pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(60)          # show long strings in full
pl.Config.set_fmt_table_cell_list_len(6)

planes_df = datasets.planes()
airports_df = datasets.airports()
flights_df = datasets.flights()

reports_df = pl.DataFrame({"report": [      # invented, report-like snippets
    "CT chest: 5 mm nodule in RUL. No pneumothorax.",
    "CXR: small left pleural effusion.",
    "CXR: no effusion or pneumothorax.",
    "MRI brain 3 T: no no acute infarct.",
    "CT: Pneumothorax, large. Nodules 3 mm and 4.5 mm.",
    "CT ช่องท้อง: ก้อนที่ตับ 2.5 ซม.",
]})
```

### Patterns per row {#sec-str-per-row}

Pass an expression as the pattern and each row gets its own. Which aircraft
tail numbers end in their carrier's code?

```{python}
tails_df = flights_df.select("carrier", "tailnum").unique().drop_nulls()

tails_df.group_by("carrier").agg(
    n_planes=pl.len(),
    ends_in_code=pl.col("tailnum").str.ends_with(pl.col("carrier")).mean().round(2),
).sort("ends_in_code", "carrier", descending=[True, False]).head(6)
```

American (`N619AA`) always does; Southwest about half the time. Not every
method takes a per-row pattern:

| Per-row expression accepted | Not accepted (Polars 2.0) |
|---|---|
| `contains`, `find`, `count_matches`, `extract`, `extract_all`, `starts_with`, `ends_with`, `split`, `strip_prefix`, `strip_suffix`, `strip_chars` | `replace` / `replace_all` **pattern**: "dynamic pattern length … not supported yet" (the replacement *value* may vary) |
| `extract_many`: a List column of keywords per row | `contains_any`: one list for all rows only ("not yet implemented") |
| numbers: `head(n)`, `slice(offset, length)`, `pad_start(length)`, `to_integer(base=)` | `extract_groups`: a `str` only (`TypeError`) |

: Verified on Polars 2.0.0 {.striped}

To drop the code from `tailnum`, `replace(pl.col("carrier"), "")` fails, but
`strip_suffix(pl.col("carrier"))` works. The string side must be a full
column too: `pl.lit("text").str.extract_all(pl.col("pattern"))` fails with a
length mismatch instead of broadcasting.

### The regex engine {#sec-str-engine}

The Rust `regex` crate guarantees matching in linear time. The price is two
features it can't offer within that guarantee:

```{python}
#| error: true
reports_df.select(pl.col("report").str.extract(r"\d+(?= mm)", 0))   # look-ahead
```

A back-reference such as `\b(\w+) \1\b` fails the same way, with "error:
backreferences are not supported". Both errors come from the regex parser,
not from the data. The workaround:
match the context instead of looking at it, and capture the part you want.

| ICU pattern | Without look-around or back-references |
|---|---|
| `\d+(?= mm)` | `extract(r"(\d+) mm", 1)` |
| `pneumothorax` not preceded by `no` | `contains("pneumothorax") & ~contains(r"\bno\b[^.]*pneumothorax")` (recipe in @sec-str-recipes) |
| `\b(\w+) \1\b` (doubled word) | split into words, compare each with the previous one |

: Workarounds {.striped}

```{python}
reports_df.select(
    "report",
    size_mm=pl.col("report").str.extract(r"(\d+(?:\.\d+)?) mm", 1),
    doubled_word=pl.col("report").str.to_lowercase().str.extract_all(r"\w+")
        .list.eval(pl.element() == pl.element().shift(1)).list.any(),
)
```

**Unicode classes.** Character classes are Unicode-aware by default. One
mixed string against several classes (a per-row pattern again):

```{python}
classes_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "pattern": [r"\d+", r"[0-9]+", r"\w+", r"\p{L}+", r"[[:alpha:]]+", r"\p{Thai}+", r"\p{Latin}+"]
})

classes_df.with_columns(text=pl.lit("CT ช่องท้อง ๑๒ mm, Ünal 7")).select(
    "pattern", matches=pl.col("text").str.extract_all(pl.col("pattern"))
)
```

- `\d` matches Thai digits (`๑๒`); `[0-9]` or `(?-u:\d)` is ASCII only.
- `\p{L}` breaks Thai words apart: tone marks and above/below vowels are
  marks (`\p{M}`), not letters. `\w` and `\p{Thai}` keep them.
- `[[:alpha:]]` is ASCII only, so `Ünal` loses its `Ü` (ICU's is Unicode).
- `\p{Thai}` is a script, so it includes Thai digits; `\X` (grapheme) is a
  parse error.

**Flags.** stringr's `regex()` options become inline flags at the start of
the pattern, or scoped to a group with `(?i:…)`:

| stringr | Polars | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `regex(p, ignore_case = TRUE)` | `(?i)p` | Unicode case folding: `(?i)ünal` matches `ÜNAL` |
| `regex(p, multiline = TRUE)` | `(?m)p` | `^` and `$` match at each line |
| `regex(p, dotall = TRUE)` | `(?s)p` | `.` also matches `\n` |
| `regex(p, comments = TRUE)` | `(?x)p` | whitespace and `# …` ignored; escape a space as `\ ` |

: Options become flags {.striped}

```{python}
note_s = pl.Series(["FINDINGS:\nSmall nodule.\nIMPRESSION:\nNo acute finding."])

{
    "no flag": note_s.str.extract(r"FINDINGS:(.*)IMPRESSION", 1).item(),
    "(?s)": note_s.str.extract(r"(?s)FINDINGS:\s*(.*?)\s*IMPRESSION", 1).item(),
    "(?m)": note_s.str.extract_all(r"(?m)^[A-Z]+:").item().to_list(),
    "(?xs)": note_s.str.extract(r"""(?xs)
        IMPRESSION: \s*   # the heading
        (.+)              # everything after it
    """, 1).item(),
}
```

Without `(?s)`, `.` stops at the newline and the match fails.

### Detect {#sec-str-detect}

Many keywords: `contains_any()` (Aho-Corasick, literal) or one regex
alternation.

```{python}
findings = ["nodule", "effusion", "pneumothorax"]
findings_re = r"(?i)\b(?:" + "|".join(map(re.escape, findings)) + ")"

reports_df.select(
    "report",
    aho=pl.col("report").str.contains_any(findings, ascii_case_insensitive=True),
    regex=pl.col("report").str.contains(findings_re),
    which=pl.col("report").str.extract_many(findings, ascii_case_insensitive=True),
)
```

| | `contains_any` / `extract_many` | `contains` with `a|b|c` |
|---|---|---|
| Patterns | literal strings | regex (escape with `re.escape()`, or `.str.escape_regex()` on a column) |
| Case-insensitive | `ascii_case_insensitive=True`: **ASCII only** | `(?i)`: Unicode |
| Word boundaries | none: `"CT"` matches inside `"CTA"` | `\b` |
| Reports which keyword | `extract_many` | `extract_all` |

: Many keywords {.striped}

Overlapping keywords: by default the match that *ends* first wins, not the
longest; `leftmost=True` takes the leftmost start, then the first-listed
keyword:

```{python}
cta_s = pl.Series(["CTA chest"])

{
    "default": cta_s.str.extract_many(["CTA", "CT", "C"]).item().to_list(),
    "leftmost=True": cta_s.str.extract_many(["CTA", "CT", "C"], leftmost=True).item().to_list(),
}
```

Rule: list longer keywords first and pass `leftmost=True`. The same applies
to `replace_many()`.

For patterns typed by users, `contains(pattern, strict=False)` turns an
invalid regex into null instead of an error.

### Extract {#sec-str-extract}

| stringr | Polars | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `str_extract(x, p)` | `extract(p, 0)` | String, the whole match |
| `str_extract(x, p, group = 1)` | `extract(p)`: group 1 is the **default** | String |
| `str_extract_all(x, p)` | `extract_all(p)` | List(String), always whole matches |
| `str_match(x, p)` | `extract_groups(p)` | Struct, one field per group, first match only |

: Extracting {.striped}

```{python}
size_re = r"(\d+(?:\.\d+)?) ?(mm|cm|ซม)"

reports_df.select(
    "report",
    group1=pl.col("report").str.extract(size_re),
    whole=pl.col("report").str.extract(size_re, 0),
    every=pl.col("report").str.extract_all(size_re),
    no_group=pl.col("report").str.extract(r"\d+ mm"),   # group 1 doesn't exist → null
)
```

`no_group` is all null and nothing warns: with the default `group_index=1`,
a pattern without a group extracts nothing. A group number that doesn't exist
does the same.

`extract_groups()` names fields after named groups, `(?<name>…)` or
`(?P<name>…)`; unnamed groups become `"1"`, `"2"`, …; `unnest()` makes them
columns (recipe in @sec-str-recipes; more in
[Reshaping](../transform/reshape.qmd#sec-rs-names)).

Every match of a group (≈ `str_match_all()`): extract all whole matches, then
run an expression on each list element with `list.eval()` (see
[Nested Data](nested.qmd)):

```{python}
reports_df.select(
    "report",
    sizes_mm=pl.col("report").str.extract_all(r"\d+(?:\.\d+)? mm")
        .list.eval(pl.element().str.extract(r"([\d.]+)").cast(pl.Float64)),
)
```

### Replace {#sec-str-replace}

The replacement string uses `$`, not `\`:

```{python}
dates_s = pl.Series(["2025-03-14"])
iso_re = r"(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})"

{
    "$3/$2/$1": dates_s.str.replace(iso_re, "$3/$2/$1").item(),
    "${d}.${m}.${y}": dates_s.str.replace(iso_re, "${d}.${m}.${y}").item(),
    "<$0>": dates_s.str.replace(r"\d+", "<$0>").item(),
    r"\3/\2/\1": dates_s.str.replace(iso_re, r"\3/\2/\1").item(),
    "$1x": dates_s.str.replace(iso_re, "$1x").item(),
    "${1}x": dates_s.str.replace(iso_re, "${1}x").item(),
    "US$$": dates_s.str.replace(iso_re, "US$$").item(),
}
```

- `\3` is not a reference: it is inserted literally.
- `$1x` refers to a group named `1x`, which doesn't exist, so it inserts
  nothing. Use braces: `${1}x`.
- A literal `$` is `$$`, or pass `literal=True`, which turns off `$`
  expansion as well as the regex. A replacement taken from a column
  (`pl.col("value")`) is expanded too.

`replace()` replaces the first match and `replace_all()` every match, as in
stringr. `n=` replaces the first *n*, but only for a literal pattern
(`replace(".", "-", literal=True, n=2)` turns `1.2.3.4` into `1-2-3.4`):

```{python}
#| error: true
pl.Series(["1 2 3 4"]).str.replace(r"\d", "#", n=2)
```

**`replace_many()`** ≈ `str_replace_all()` with a named vector, with three
differences: patterns are literal, all of them are applied in **one pass**,
and a single replacement must still be a list:

```{python}
exam_s = pl.Series(["CT and MRI"])

{
    "mapping (swap)": exam_s.str.replace_many({"CT": "MRI", "MRI": "CT"}).item(),
    "many → one": exam_s.str.replace_many(["CT", "MRI"], ["<scan>"]).item(),
}
```

stringr applies a named vector in turn, so
`str_replace_all("CT and MRI", c(CT = "MRI", MRI = "CT"))` gives
`"CT and CT"`. One pass makes the swap work. A bare string as the
replacement (`replace_many(["CT", "MRI"], "<scan>")`) raises "Use `implode`
to wrap the string value into a list"; and a bare string as the *patterns*
argument is read as a column name (@sec-str-gotchas).

### Length and Unicode {#sec-str-unicode}

```{python}
organs_df = pl.DataFrame({"word": ["ปอด", "ท้อง", "น้ำ", "กระดูกสันหลัง", "lung", "café"]})

organs_df.with_columns(
    chars=pl.col("word").str.len_chars(),
    bytes=pl.col("word").str.len_bytes(),
    head2=pl.col("word").str.head(2),
    slice_1_1=pl.col("word").str.slice(1, 1),
    reversed=pl.col("word").str.reverse(),
)
```

```text
 ท้อง  =  ท       ◌้        อ       ง          len_chars() = 4  (code points; = str_length())
         U+0E17  U+0E49    U+0E2D  U+0E07     len_bytes() = 12 (3 bytes each in UTF-8)
         letter  mark (Mn) letter  letter     what you see = 3 cells
```

- `len_chars()` counts code points, like `str_length()`, so a tone mark or
  above/below vowel counts as a character.
- `head()`, `tail()` and `slice()` cut between code points: `slice(1, 1)` of
  `ท้อง` is a lone tone mark; `head(2)` of `น้ำ` drops the final vowel.
- `reverse()` is the exception: it keeps a base character and its marks
  together (`งอท้`, where a code-point reversal gives `งอ้ท`).
- Polars has no grapheme-cluster length (`\X` is not supported). The number
  of visible cells is close to `len_chars() - count_matches(r"\p{Mn}")`.

**`find()` returns a byte offset**, while `slice()` takes characters. On
ASCII the two agree; on Thai they don't:

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"s": ["CT chest 5 mm", "CT ช่องท้อง 5 mm"]}).with_columns(
    at=pl.col("s").str.find(r"\d"),
    sliced=pl.col("s").str.slice(pl.col("s").str.find(r"\d")),   # wrong on Thai
    extracted=pl.col("s").str.extract(r"(\d.*)", 1),             # right
)
```

`find_many()` returns bytes too. To cut at a pattern, extract or split with a
regex instead of computing an offset.

**Normalization.** One visible string can have several encodings, and they
compare unequal. Two spellings each of `café` and Thai `คำ`:

```{python}
variants_df = pl.DataFrame({"term": ["caf\u00e9", "cafe\u0301", "ค\u0e33", "ค\u0e4d\u0e32"]})

variants_df.select(
    distinct_raw=pl.col("term").n_unique(),
    distinct_nfc=pl.col("term").str.normalize("NFC").n_unique(),
    distinct_nfkc=pl.col("term").str.normalize("NFKC").n_unique(),
)
```

`é` precomposed (U+00E9) and `e` + combining acute (U+0301) become one under
NFC. Thai SARA AM (`ำ`, U+0E33) and NIKHAHIT + SARA AA (`ํ` + `า`), a common
typing variant of the same vowel, become one only under NFKC, because SARA
AM's decomposition is a compatibility one. Normalize the patterns as well:
after NFKC, a literal `"คำ"` typed in Python no longer matches the column
(`unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", "คำ")` does).

**Case.**

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"s": ["straße", "mri ของ สมอง", "x-ray of l1", "ct3d DICOM-RT", "o'neil mcdonald"]}).with_columns(
    upper=pl.col("s").str.to_uppercase(),
    title=pl.col("s").str.to_titlecase(),
)
```

Case mapping is full Unicode (`ß` → `SS`, so the length changes) and Thai,
which has no case, passes through. `to_titlecase()` starts a new word after
any character that is not a letter, so digits, hyphens and apostrophes
restart capitalisation (`Ct3D`, `Dicom-Rt`, `O'Neil`), and acronyms are
lowercased.

### Shaping {#sec-str-shaping}

**Strip.** `strip_chars()` takes a *set* of characters and removes any of
them from both ends; `strip_prefix()` / `strip_suffix()` remove one literal
string, once:

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"s": ["CTCT scan CT", "\u00a0 CT chest \t", "007", "000"]}).with_columns(
    chars_CT=pl.col("s").str.strip_chars("CT"),
    prefix_CT=pl.col("s").str.strip_prefix("CT"),
    whitespace=pl.col("s").str.strip_chars(),          # any Unicode whitespace, incl. NBSP
    zeros=pl.col("s").str.strip_chars_start("0"),      # "000" → ""
)
```

**Pad.** Padding counts characters (code points) and takes a single fill
character; `zfill()` knows about signs:

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"s": ["7", "-7", "12345", "ปอด"]}).with_columns(
    pad_start=pl.col("s").str.pad_start(4, "0"),
    zfill=pl.col("s").str.zfill(4),
    pad_end=pl.col("s").str.pad_end(4, "."),
)
```

**Slice.** 0-based `(offset, length)`: `str_sub(s, 3, 5)` is `slice(2, 3)`.
A negative `n` means "all but": `head(-2)` ≈ `str_sub(s, 1, -3)` and
`tail(-2)` ≈ `str_sub(s, 3)`. An offset past the end gives `""`; a negative
`length` in `slice()` is an error.

**Interpolate.** `pl.format()` accepts glue-style named placeholders, which
refer to columns directly, as well as `{}` (next argument) and `{0}` (by
position):

```{python}
exams_df = pl.DataFrame({"modality": ["CT", "MRI", None], "region": ["chest", "brain", "knee"], "slice_mm": [5.0, 1.25, 3.0]})

exams_df.select(
    named=pl.format("{modality} {region}, {slice_mm} mm"),
    positional=pl.format("{} ({})", "region", "modality"),
)
```

Unlike glue, a placeholder is a column name only: no expressions, no format
specs (`{:.2f}` fails with "unacceptable column name"), and the name must be
an ASCII identifier. A null input gives a null row, as with `pl.concat_str()`
(see [Missing Values](missing.qmd#sec-na-propagation)).

**Numbers ↔ strings.** Parsing is strict and literal: no surrounding spaces,
no thousands separators, no Thai digits:

```{python}
thai_digits = dict(zip("๐๑๒๓๔๕๖๗๘๙", "0123456789"))

pl.DataFrame({"s": ["42", " 7", "1,234", "3.5", "๑๒", "ff"]}).with_columns(
    int=pl.col("s").str.to_integer(strict=False),
    float=pl.col("s").cast(pl.Float64, strict=False),
    cleaned=pl.col("s").str.strip_chars().str.replace_all(",", "", literal=True)
        .str.replace_many(thai_digits).str.to_integer(strict=False),
    hex=pl.col("s").str.to_integer(base=16, strict=False),
)
```

With `strict=True` (the default) any bad value raises an error. `base=`
also accepts an expression, and `"0x1A"` with `base=16` fails: prefixes are
not stripped. Going the other way there is no `sprintf()`: casting a float
to `String` drops trailing zeros. Casting through `Decimal` fixes the number
of decimals:

```{python}
pl.DataFrame({"x": [3.14159, 2.0, 0.1 + 0.2]}).with_columns(
    plain=pl.col("x").cast(pl.String),
    rounded=pl.col("x").round(2).cast(pl.String),
    fixed2=pl.col("x").cast(pl.Decimal(scale=2)).cast(pl.String),
)
```

## Where it bites {#sec-str-gotchas}

| stringr habit | Polars 2.0 | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| a `"."` meant literally | `contains(".")` is a regex: matches every non-empty string | `literal=True` |
| `str_extract(x, p)` gives the match | `extract(p)` gives group 1, so null without a group | `extract(p, 0)` |
| `\\1` in a replacement | `\1` is inserted literally; `$1x` is a group named `1x` | `$1`, `${1}x` |
| `str_replace_all()` with a named vector | `replace_many()` matches substrings, not words | regex with `\b` |
| look-around, back-references | parse error | capture groups (@sec-str-engine) |
| `str_sub()` is 1-based | 0-based `(offset, length)` | |
| `str_locate()` gives character positions | `find()` gives byte offsets | `extract()` |
| `[[:alpha:]]` is Unicode | ASCII only | `\p{L}`, `\w`, `\p{Thai}` |
| `\b` around a Thai word | Thai has no spaces between words | no `\b` in Thai text |
| `str_length(a) - str_length(b)` can be negative | `UInt32` wraps: `ปอด` − `ท้อง` = 4294967295 ([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-unsigned)) | cast to `Int64` first |
| a string argument is a value | `contains_any("x")` reads `"x"` as a column | pass a list |
| stringr works on factors | `.str` on a `Categorical` raises "expected String type, got: cat" ([Categorical & Enum](categorical.qmd)) | `cast(pl.String)` |

: The differences at a glance {.striped}

### `"."` matches everything {#sec-str-dot}

```{python}
pl.Series(["v1.2", "v102", "v1-2"]).str.contains("1.2").to_list()
```

### `replace_many()` has no word boundaries {#sec-str-substrings}

Expanding the abbreviations in `airports.name` (`Intl`, `Rgnl`, `Muni`, …)
with `replace_many()` also rewrites every word that *contains* one:

```{python}
abbreviations = {"Intl": "International", "Rgnl": "Regional", "Muni": "Municipal", "Fld": "Field", "Co": "County"}

name_expanded = pl.col("name")
for short, full in abbreviations.items():
    name_expanded = name_expanded.str.replace_all(rf"\b{short}\b", full)

airports_df_damaged = airports_df.select(
    "faa", "name",
    aho=pl.col("name").str.replace_many(abbreviations),
    regex=name_expanded,
).filter(pl.col("aho") != pl.col("regex"))

print(airports_df_damaged.height, "names damaged")
airports_df_damaged.sort("faa").select("faa", "aho", "regex").head(3)
```

`replace_all()` takes one pattern, so the regex fix chains one call per
abbreviation (built in a loop, see
[Expressions](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-recipes)).

### `\b` and Thai {#sec-str-thai-boundary}

`\w` includes Thai letters and Thai is written without spaces, so a Thai word
is almost never between two word boundaries:

```{python}
lung_s = pl.Series(["ปอดอักเสบ", "ไม่พบความผิดปกติของปอด", "ปอด ปกติ"])

{
    r"\bปอด\b": lung_s.str.contains(r"\bปอด\b").to_list(),
    "ปอด": lung_s.str.contains("ปอด").to_list(),
}
```

Substring search over-matches instead (`ปอด` "lung" is inside many longer
words). Precise Thai matching needs word segmentation, which Polars doesn't do.

### Strings that are column names {#sec-str-colname}

```{python}
#| error: true
reports_df.select(pl.col("report").str.contains_any("effusion"))
```

`contains_any()`, `extract_many()` and `replace_many()` take their patterns
as expression input, so a bare string is a column (the rule in
[Expressions](../core/expressions.qmd#sec-expr-literals)). A list is a value.

## Recipes {#sec-str-recipes}

**Collapse manufacturer variants** in `planes` (`AIRBUS` vs `AIRBUS
INDUSTRIE`). One anchored regex removes any run of company suffixes; list
longer alternatives before their prefixes:

```{python}
suffix_re = r"(?: (?:INDUSTRIE|AIRCRAFT CO|CORPORATION|CORP|INC|LTD|CO))+$"

planes_df_clean = planes_df.with_columns(maker=pl.col("manufacturer").str.replace(suffix_re, ""))
print(planes_df["manufacturer"].n_unique(), "→", planes_df_clean["maker"].n_unique())

with pl.Config(fmt_str_lengths=90, tbl_width_chars=120):
    print(
        planes_df_clean.group_by("maker").agg(
            n=pl.len(),
            variants=pl.col("manufacturer").unique().sort().str.join(" | "),
        ).filter(pl.col("variants").str.contains("|", literal=True)).sort("maker")
    )
```

Three makers absorb seven spellings. The `$` anchor is not decorative: without
it, `" CO"` cuts into any word that starts with `CO` (`"ACME COMPANY CO"`
→ `"ACMEMPANY CO"`).

**A number with its unit, from free text in two languages.** Translate Thai
digits first, then capture value and unit, then convert:

```{python}
findings_df = pl.DataFrame({"finding": [
    "CT chest: 5 mm slices",
    "Nodule 0.6cm in RUL",
    "Thyroid nodule 12.5 mm, TI-RADS 3",
    "ก้อนที่ตับ ขนาด ๑.๕ ซม.",
    "No measurable lesion",
]})
mm_per_unit = {"mm": 1, "มม": 1, "cm": 10, "ซม": 10}

findings_df.with_columns(
    size=pl.col("finding").str.replace_many(thai_digits)
        .str.extract_groups(r"(?<value>\d+(?:\.\d+)?)\s*(?<unit>mm|cm|มม|ซม)")
).unnest("size").with_columns(
    size_mm=pl.col("value").cast(pl.Float64) * pl.col("unit").replace_strict(mm_per_unit),
)
```

**Detect findings, excluding negated ones.** A finding counts if it is
mentioned and no `no` precedes it in the same sentence. Without look-behind,
the negation is a second pattern that includes its context:

```{python}
reports_df.with_columns(**{
    finding: pl.col("report").str.contains(rf"(?i)\b{finding}")
    & ~pl.col("report").str.contains(rf"(?i)\bno\b[^.]*\b{finding}")
    for finding in findings
})
```

`No pneumothorax.` after a nodule and `no effusion or pneumothorax` are both
excluded; `Nodules` counts because the pattern has no closing `\b`. Real
negation detection (NegEx-style) needs more rules than this.

**Split Thai and English parts** of a bilingual label: two extractions by
script, rejoined:

```{python}
labels_df = pl.DataFrame({"label": [
    "ปอดอักเสบ Pneumonia",
    "Pleural effusion น้ำในช่องเยื่อหุ้มปอด",
    "CT ช่องท้อง (abdomen)",
]})

labels_df.with_columns(
    thai=pl.col("label").str.extract_all(r"\p{Thai}+(?:\s+\p{Thai}+)*").list.join(" "),
    english=pl.col("label").str.extract_all(r"\p{Latin}+(?:\s+\p{Latin}+)*").list.join(" "),
)
```

`\p{Thai}` also matches Thai digits; use `[\p{Thai}--\p{Nd}]` (class
subtraction) to leave them out.
